title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to test whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated device configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as the generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, every single shared generated candidate was verifier‑accepted: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify→optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was never invoked. Observed paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false), which makes the run’s contingency degenerate; we document the exact preregistration, execution manifest, scoring artifacts, and provide a minimal reproducible recipe (artifact‑anchored) for testing the original independent‑sampling estimand.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can translate high‑level NetOps intent into device configuration, but stochastic generation raises safety concerns when outputs touch network control planes. A common operational architecture to constrain stochasticity is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): probabilistic generation followed by deterministic verification and, if rejected, a bounded LLM‑guided repair loop that uses verifier diagnostics. We preregistered a confirmatory paired within‑task study (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to measure the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic network verifier into an LLM pipeline on detection/rejection rates and bounded repair success. The experimental design, data, execution traces, and all scoring/validator outputs are archived with SHA‑256 manifests to support deterministic reproduction (see Disclosure and artifact pointers). The central research question: does embedding a formal network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase the proportion of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated configurations that are detected/rejected and, when rejected, does a bounded repair succeed more often than single‑shot generation?
sections.related_work: Prior work proposes GVR architectures in compliance‑sensitive domains to bound LLM hallucination and enforce deterministic checks (e.g., Cadenas’ formalization of GVR for convergent correctness; doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899). Formal network verification frameworks (NetKAT family and weighted NetKAT decision procedures) provide candidate deterministic oracles for network properties (see Suárez Acevedo et al., doi:10.1145/3808318). Recent LLM→NetOps proposals focus on intent life‑cycle, retrieval anchors, and verifier integration (OpenAlex entries W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061), but published empirical evidence with preregistration, deterministic logging, and paired estimands is limited. Our contribution is an artifact‑anchored, preregistered paired experiment with full per‑episode validator traces and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes, enabling deterministic inspection of the exact runs that produced the reported contingency.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan: The preregistration (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0) specified estimands, sampling, retry policy, repair budget, and the decisive generation semantics. Key registered elements: generator = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) executed against a Kathará/Mininet emulator (emulator ground truth declared), task bank SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1 (270 tasks), and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Design decisions enacted at execution: paired within‑task (Npairs=270), shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false), one shared generated candidate per task evaluated in both baseline and guarded arms, model_calls_used=270, maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. Execution artifact provenance: full execution manifest, raw responses, provider traces, and scoring JSONs archived (execution/*; raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a). Scoring and verification: each candidate was deterministically validated; scoring JSONs include validator_traces (final_configuration, parsed_command_count, violations) for every episode (examples in execution/scoring/*.json). Statistical analysis: primary test = paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided), paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (seed=1729). Missingness and retries: preregistered retry policy (≤2 retries per failed model call); no retries were required in this run (failed_hosted_model_call_event_count=0).
sections.results: Execution and counts (artifact‑anchored). Planned episodes: 540 (270 paired tasks × 2 conditions). Completed episodes: 540; failed: 0. Model calls used: 270 (one shared generation per pair as preregistered). Observed contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 62cd99d7...): n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (baseline accepted 270/270; guarded accepted 270/270). Repair invocation: 0 (guarded path not invoked because verifier accepted every shared candidate). Inference: observed paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Representative scoring JSONs and validator traces for example episodes are archived (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2e...).
sections.discussion: Interpretation and methodological diagnosis. The run produced a provenance‑backed null because (A) the executed generation semantics evaluated a single shared candidate per paired task (independent_condition_generation=false) and (B) the chosen generator/prompt/settings produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for the supplied synthetic tasks. Under these conditions there were zero discordant pairs, so the McNemar test and bootstrap CI are arithmetically degenerate (p=1.0; CI=[0.00,0.00]); the analysis artifacts record this exact contingency (analysis/*). This outcome does not imply deterministic verifiers are unnecessary in general; it identifies a concrete regime (low generator failure rate + shared candidate semantics) where inserting a verifier and a bounded repair loop produces no measured marginal effect on accept/reject outcomes. Relation to preregistration and power: the preregistered MDE/power calculation assumed independent per‑arm sampling; that assumption does not hold under shared_initial_candidate semantics, therefore the original power statements are inapplicable to the observed contingency. Reproducible minimal follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored) to test the original independent‑sampling estimand: change only these preregistered JSON fields and re‑run the archived harness (paths shown in execution/*): (1) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = true so each arm receives an independent stochastic generation; (2) set planned_model_calls or maximum_model_calls to >=540 so independent generation per arm is permitted (execution_manifest documents model_calls_used and maximum_model_calls); (3) set execution/model_configuration.json temperature to a nonzero value or provide explicit per‑task generation seeds to induce sampling variability; (4) optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1 to test bounded repair convergence. All referenced field names, JSON paths, and artifact locations are present in the archived preregistration and execution manifest (see Disclosure). Threats to validity. Internal: shared candidate semantics removed between‑arm stochasticity and altered the estimand; construct: synthetic tasks approximate operational intent patterns but lack vendor/real‑traffic heterogeneity; external: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and single verifier rule set; conclusion: degenerate contingency precludes rejecting the null and invalidates the preregistered power interpretation for independent sampling. Operational implication: pipeline authors and evaluators must treat generation semantics (shared vs independent sampling) as an explicit design choice because it directly controls whether a verifier can change observed outcomes in paired tests.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released the full execution, scoring, and analysis bundle with per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifests. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for all N=270 tasks, so the verifier/repair path was not invoked and the measured paired difference is 0.00. The principal scientific lesson is methodological: whether a verifier can effect observed change depends crucially on generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) and on generator failure rate for the chosen task bank. We publish a compact, deterministic recipe (artifact‑anchored) to re‑exercise the preregistered estimand under independent sampling and invite reproduction using the archived harness and per‑artifact hashes. All raw outputs, per‑episode validator traces, execution logs, and the full SHA‑256 manifest are released to permit deterministic inspection and minimal follow‑ups (see Disclosure and artifact pointers).

limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments; emulator behavior can differ from heterogeneous production devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality is made.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and thereby eliminated between‑arm stochastic sampling variance; the preregistered MDE/power calculations assumed independent sampling and are therefore inapplicable to the observed contingency.

Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: a single deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and rule set were used; different verifier conservatism or policy choices will change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or multi‑vendor deployments.
